A **neutral point** is where the coil's field exactly cancels the Earth's horizontal
field.
**Step 1 — state the condition.** At the centre of the coil the two fields are equal and
opposite:
B_coil = **B_H** = 0·314 x 10⁻⁴ T ✓
**Step 2 — write the field at the centre of the coil.**
B_coil = μ₀NI/(2r) ✓
**Step 3 — equate and solve for I.**
μ₀NI/(2r) = B_H
I = 2rB_H/(μ₀N)
**Step 4 — substitute.**
I = 2(0·1)(0·314 x 10⁻⁴)/[(4π x 10⁻⁷)(10)]
= (6·28 x 10⁻⁶)/(1·2566 x 10⁻⁵)
= **0·5 A** ✓
**Why the geometry works.** The coil's plane is **normal to the magnetic meridian**, so
the coil's own field - which is perpendicular to its plane - lies **along** the
meridian, parallel or antiparallel to B_H ✓ Only in that orientation can the two cancel
exactly.
**A check on the arithmetic.**
μ₀N/(2r) = (4π x 10⁻⁷)(10)/(0·2) = **6·28 x 10⁻⁵ T A⁻¹**
so I = 0·314 x 10⁻⁴/(6·28 x 10⁻⁵) = **0·5 A** ✓
**Why 0·314 x 10⁻⁴ T is chosen.** It is **10⁻⁴/π** T, which makes the π in μ₀ cancel
neatly ✓ Such values are picked so the arithmetic comes out round.
**What a neutral point means in practice.** A compass needle placed exactly at the
centre of the coil would point **anywhere** - there is no resultant field to align
it ✓ Moving slightly away, the cancellation fails and the needle settles again.
**A realistic value for B_H.** The Earth's horizontal field in southern India is about
**0·4 x 10⁻⁴ T**, so 0·314 x 10⁻⁴ T is entirely plausible ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **1 A** ✗ and **2 A** ✗ would produce fields of 6·28 x 10⁻⁵
and 1·26 x 10⁻⁴ T, overwhelming the Earth's field rather than cancelling it. **0·25 A**
✗ gives only half the required field ✓
∴ 0.5 A.

Use the turns ratio for the **voltage** and the efficiency for the **power**.
**Step 1 — find the secondary voltage.** With a turns ratio of 3 in the step-up sense,
V_s = 3V_p
= 3(100)
= **300 V** ✓
**Step 2 — find the input power.**
P_in = V_p I_p
= 100 x 2
= **200 W**
**Step 3 — apply the efficiency.**
P_out = η P_in
= 0·75 x 200
= **150 W** ✓
**Step 4 — find the secondary current.**
I_s = P_out/V_s
= 150/300
= **0·5 A** ✓
**Why the efficiency must be applied to the power, not the voltage.** The turns ratio
fixes the **voltage** exactly, by Faraday's law ✓ Losses - in the winding resistance, in
eddy currents and in hysteresis - show up as **missing power**, which means a smaller
secondary **current** than an ideal transformer would give.
**The ideal comparison.** A perfect transformer would deliver
I_s = I_p/3 = **0·667 A** at 300 V, that is **200 W** ✓
The 75% efficiency reduces that to 0·5 A, losing **50 W** as heat in the core and
windings.
**Where the lost 50 W goes.**
**copper loss**, I²R in the windings
**eddy-current loss**, reduced by laminating the core
**hysteresis loss**, reduced by using soft iron ✓
A good modern transformer reaches 95-99%; 75% is poor, chosen here to make the
arithmetic clear.
**A consistency check.**
output: 300 x 0·5 = **150 W**
input: 100 x 2 = **200 W**
efficiency: 150/200 = **0·75** ✓ exactly as given.
**Reading the distractors.** **300 V, 1·5 A** ✗ would be 450 W out of 200 W in - more
energy out than in. **150 V, 1·5 A** ✗ and **150 V, 0·5 A** ✗ use the turns ratio
wrongly on the voltage ✓ The first of these also violates conservation of energy.
∴ 300 V, 0.5 A.

A rising current in A induces a current in B that **opposes** it - and anti-parallel
currents **repel**.
**Step 1 — find the flux through B.** Coil A's current produces a magnetic field that
threads coil B, and since the current is **increasing**, that flux is **increasing** ✓
**Step 2 — apply Lenz's law.** The induced current in B opposes the **increase**, so it
flows in the direction that produces a field **opposing** A's ✓ That means B's induced
current circulates **opposite** to A's current.
**Step 3 — find the force.** Two coils carrying currents in **opposite** senses
**repel** each other ✓ So coil B is **repelled**.
**Step 4 — confirm with the energy argument.** Lenz's law is conservation of energy in
disguise ✓ If B were attracted, it would accelerate towards A, increasing the flux
further and strengthening the induced current - energy from nothing. Repulsion is the
only possibility.
**The current rule for parallel conductors.**
**same direction** → **attract** ✓
**opposite directions** → **repel** ✓
The same rule applies to coils, treated as stacks of parallel current loops.
**What happens if the current in A instead decreases.** The flux through B falls, the
induced current flows the **same** way as A's to maintain it, and B is **attracted** ✓
The direction of the force follows the **rate of change**, not the current itself.
**What happens at a steady current.** No change of flux, **no** induced emf and **no**
induced current in B ✓ With no current in B there is no force on it at all - the force
exists only while A's current is changing.
**The practical application.** This is the principle of the **induction launcher** and
of the jumping-ring demonstration ✓ A ring placed over an a.c.-fed coil is thrown
upward, because the induced current in the ring opposes the coil's and the two repel.
**Reading the distractors.** "**attracted by A**" ✗ reverses Lenz's law. "**remains
stationary**" ✗ would need no induced current, but the flux is changing. "**rotates**" ✗
would need a **torque**, which requires a misalignment the symmetric arrangement does
not have ✓
∴ is repelled.

Mutual inductance relates the induced emf to the **rate of change** of the current in the
other coil.
**Step 1 — write the relation.**
e = −M (di/dt) ✓
**Step 2 — differentiate the current.** With i = i_m sin ωt:
di/dt = i_m ω cos ωt ✓
**Step 3 — find the maximum.** The cosine reaches 1, so
|e|_max = M i_m ω ✓
**Step 4 — substitute.**
e_max = (0·005)(10)(100π)
= 0·05 x 100π
= **5π volt** ✓
**The numerical value.** 5π = **15·7 V** ✓
**Why ω enters the answer.** The emf depends on how **fast** the current changes, not
how large it is ✓ The same 10 A amplitude at twice the frequency would induce twice the
emf - which is why high-frequency circuits need careful shielding against mutual
coupling.
**When the emf is greatest.** At the instants the current passes through **zero** ✓
There cos ωt = ±1 and the current is changing fastest. At the current's peaks, di/dt = 0
and the induced emf is **zero** - the two are 90° out of phase.
**What mutual inductance measures.** The flux linked with coil 2 per unit current in coil
1:
M = N₂Φ₂/I₁ ✓
It depends only on the **geometry** of the two coils and the medium between them - their
sizes, separation, orientation and whether an iron core links them.
**The reciprocity theorem.** M₁₂ = M₂₁ **always** ✓ A current in either coil links the
same flux per ampere with the other, however different their sizes - a result that is
far from obvious and is proved from energy considerations.
**Where this matters.** It is the whole basis of the **transformer**, and the cause of
unwanted **cross-talk** between nearby circuits ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **2π**, **π** and **4π** ✗ correspond to products Mi_mω of
0·02, 0·01 and 0·04 ✓ Only 0·005 x 10 x 100 = 5 gives 5π, and the multiplication is the
whole of the calculation.
∴ 5 π.

Magnetic braking works by **eddy currents** induced in the moving metal.
**Step 1 — describe the arrangement.** An electromagnet is placed near the train's metal
rail or a disc attached to the wheels ✓ As the metal moves through the field, the flux
through each small region of it **changes**.
**Step 2 — see what is induced.** A changing flux through a bulk conductor drives
circulating currents within the metal itself - **eddy currents** ✓ They need no circuit;
the metal provides its own closed paths.
**Step 3 — apply Lenz's law.** The eddy currents flow in the sense that **opposes the
motion** producing them ✓ The result is a retarding force proportional to the speed, so
the train is smoothly slowed.
**Why eddy-current braking is attractive.**
**no contact**, so **no wear** on brake pads or discs ✓
**smooth and silent**, with no jerk
**self-limiting**, since the force falls with the speed
**no fade** from overheating, unlike friction brakes
**Its one limitation.** The force is proportional to **speed**, so it dies away as the
train slows and cannot hold it at rest ✓ A conventional friction brake is still needed
for the final stop and for parking.
**Where the kinetic energy goes.** The eddy currents dissipate it as **heat** in the
metal, through I²R ✓ In a **regenerative** system the same principle is run as a
generator and the energy is returned to the supply instead.
**Other uses of eddy currents.** Induction furnaces, induction cooktops, metal
detectors, and the damping of moving-coil galvanometers ✓ The same effect is a
**nuisance** in transformer cores, where it is suppressed by laminating the iron.
**Why the other options are wrong.** **Alternating**, **steady** and **pulsating**
current ✗ describe currents supplied **to** a circuit; eddy currents are **induced**
within the body of the metal itself, and that induction is the whole mechanism ✓ The
electromagnet may well be fed with steady current - it is the **motion** that generates
the braking.
∴ eddy current.

Inserting an iron rod raises the coil's **inductance**, raising its reactance and
cutting the current.
**Step 1 — see what the rod does to the inductance.**
L = μ₀μ_r N²A/l ✓
Iron has a relative permeability μ_r of several hundred to several thousand, so
inserting the rod increases **L** enormously.
**Step 2 — see what that does to the reactance.**
X_L = ωL ✓
With L larger, the inductive reactance **increases**.
**Step 3 — see what that does to the current.**
Z = √(R² + X_L²), and I = V/Z ✓
A larger X_L gives a larger impedance and hence a **smaller** current.
**Step 4 — conclude.** Less current through the bulb means less power, so the bulb
**glows less brightly** ✓
**Why the brightness depends on the current.** For the filament,
P = I²R ✓
so even a modest fall in current cuts the power sharply - halving the current quarters
the brightness.
**Why this works only on a.c.** The reactance is ωL, which is **zero** for direct
current ✓ On a d.c. supply the coil is merely a length of wire and the rod makes no
difference at all once the current is steady. The question's "A.C." is essential.
**The classic demonstration.** This is the standard lecture experiment showing that an
**inductor chokes** alternating current ✓ Sliding the iron core in and out dims and
brightens the lamp smoothly, with no switch and - ideally - no power wasted in the coil.
**Where it is used.** A **choke** in a fluorescent lamp circuit limits the current
without the heat a resistor would produce ✓ and a **variable** inductor of exactly this
kind was once used as a stage-lighting dimmer.
**What happens to the power factor.** It falls, since cos φ = R/Z and Z has risen ✓ The
circuit becomes more reactive, and more of the apparent power is merely exchanged with
the coil rather than consumed.
**Reading the distractors.** "**More brightly**" ✗ would need the impedance to fall.
"**Same brightness**" ✗ would need the inductance to be unchanged. "**Gets damaged**" ✗
would need **more** current, not less ✓
∴ glows less brightly.
